Content: Measures of center are statistical tools used to summarize an entire dataset with a single value that is representative of the entire distribution. While looking at a long list of numbers can be overwhelming, a measure of center distills that complexity into an quantitative snapshot that precisely captures the middle or average of a dataset. In the real world, this type of measure makes sense of large-scale trends. Economists use the median household income to understand the financial security of a population and restaurants track average daily orders to predict how many ingredients to keep in stock.

On the SAT, being proficient with measures of center is critical for success in the Problem Solving and Data Analysis category. Beyond simply calculating a value, many SAT problems will evaluate our understanding of how these metrics behave under different conditions. The goal can range from finding the median of a complex frequency table to determining how an additional data point changes the average to predicting which measure of center is best suited for a heavily skewed dataset. Learning the distinct purposes of the mean, median, and mode is required to interpret distributions whether they are quantitative or visual.

The first and most common metric is the mean, otherwise known as the average. Calculate the mean involves adding up all the individual values in a dataset and dividing that sum by the total number of data points. The formula is written as `text(Mean)=(sumx)/n`, What defines the mean is that it is like the center of gravity for a dataset and every single value plays an equal role in determining its value. Due to this fact, the mean is highly sensitive to outliers — extreme values far away from the rest of the dataset. A single value that is abnormally high or low will pull the mean sharply toward it, which has potential to result in a summary value that doesn't reflect the majority of the group.

The median solves this outlier effect by focusing purely on the position of actual data points rather than an average. The median is the number that falls exactly in the middle when a dataset is arranged in order from least to greatest. If a dataset has an odd number of values, the median is the single data point directly in the center. If the dataset has an even number of values, the median is the average of the two middle values in the dataset. By relying on the data points in the middle, the median is not affected by more extreme data values at either end of the distribution. If a neighborhood consists of five small homes worth `text($250,000)`and one mansion worth `text($4,000,000)`, the median home value remains representative at `text($250,000)` but the expensive mansion would raise the mean to `text($1,000,000)`.

The final measure of center is the mode, which is simply the value that appears most frequently in a dataset. A distribution can have one mode, multiple modes (if two or more values are tied for highest frequency), or no mode at all (if all values appear with equal frequency). While the mean and median only work numerical data, the mode is more robust and can be applied to categorical data - like the most popular color of car sold at a dealership.

The SAT exam includes problems designed to test our understanding of shape and skewness by describing various relationships between the mean and median. When a dataset is perfectly symmetrical, the mean and the median will equal the exact same value. However, graphs that feature a long tail stretching to the right (known as a right-skewed distribution) due to high-value outliers indicate that `text(mean)>text(median)`. Conversely, left-skewed distribution with a long tail of low-value outliers mean that `text(mean)<text(median)`. A shortcut when presented with these visual cues is that the skews toward the direction of the tail..
